verdict.summary:
# AC-7 (Unsuccessful Logon Attempts) — what Rev. 5 actually requires

## Answer

**NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AC-7, requires no specific number of attempts, no specific time window, and no specific lockout duration.** All three are *Assignment* (and, for the response, *Selection*) operations that the organization must fill in. The control is a requirement to *have* a limit and *have* an automatic response — not a requirement to use particular figures.

Verbatim control text (from the NIST CSRC Rev. 5 controls export, sha256 6fc1c2414396):

> **AC-7 Unsuccessful Logon Attempts**
> a. Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; and
> b. Automatically [Selection (one or more): lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; lock the account or node until released by an administrator; delay next logon prompt per [Assignment: organization-defined delay algorithm]; notify system administrator; take other [Assignment: organization-defined action].

So the three questions map to the control like this:

| Ask | What AC-7 says | Who supplies the value |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Number of consecutive invalid logon attempts | `[Assignment: organization-defined number]` | The organization, documented in its security plan / policy |
| 2. Time period within which they must occur | `[Assignment: organization-defined time period]` | The organization |
| 3. Lockout duration | `[Assignment: organization-defined time period]` — **only if** the organization selects the “lock for a period” option; the other four selections are valid alternatives | The organization |

Note on ask 3 in particular: AC-7b is a *Selection*, not a single mandatory response. An organization that selects “lock the account until released by an administrator” has **no** lockout duration at all. There is therefore no single correct answer to ask 3 even in principle — the control permits five distinct responses, only one of which has a duration.

## Why you may have seen “3 attempts / 15 minutes / 15-minute lockout”

The figure 3-15-15 circulates widely and is often attributed to NIST SP 800-53. It is **not in AC-7 and not in AC-7’s enhancements.** The Rev. 5 enhancements are written the same parameterized way — e.g. AC-7(1) Automatic Account Lockout likewise takes an organization-defined number of consecutive invalid attempts rather than a constant, and AC-7(4) Use of Alternate Authentication Factor (quoted from the same source) is entirely `[Assignment: organization-defined …]`:

> AC-7(4) … (a) Allow the use of [Assignment: organization-defined authentication factors] that are different from the primary authentication factors after the number of organization-defined consecutive invalid logon attempts have been exceeded; and (b) Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts through use of the alternative factors by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period].

The 3-15-15 figure is an *organizational/vendor* choice (it appears in DISA STIGs and in many agency security plans and commercial defaults). It is a defensible choice, but citing AC-7 for it is a misattribution. To my knowledge, SP 800-53B scopes *which* controls and enhancements apply at each impact baselining (AC-7 is in the low baselining and above) but does not substitute numbers for AC-7’s assignments — **verify this against the current 800-53B before relying on it**, since baselining overlays are revised independently of the control catalog.

## What the organization must actually do

1. **Assign and document** the three parameters (plus the AC-7b selection) in the system security plan and in the organization’s policy. That documented value — not a NIST constant — is what an assessor tests against under SP 800-53A (AC-07a / AC-07b).
2. **Pick a response that fits the threat model.** The AC-7(4) discussion text (quoted above) makes the trade-off explicit: alternate factors “support the objective of availability and allow a user who has inadvertently been locked out” to recover — i.e. lockout is a denial-of-service vector against a known username, which is why AC-7b offers delay algorithms and administrator release as alternatives to hard lockout.
3. **Do not treat “no NIST number” as “no requirement.”** AC-7 is a real, assessable control: an account with unlimited attempts, or with a limit but no automatic response, fails regardless of which numbers are chosen.

## Implementation: making the three parameters configurable (backend)

Because the values are organizational inputs, the correct engineering pattern is a policy object, not hard-coded constants. Minimal schema:

```json
{
  "policy_id": "ac7-default",
  "max_consecutive_invalid_attempts": 3,          // AC-7a [Assignment] — ORG CHOICE, not NIST
  "attempt_window_seconds": 900,                   // AC-7a [Assignment] — 15 min, ORG CHOICE
  "counting_scope": "per_user_id",                 // or per_user_id+source_ip
  "response": {
    "type": "lock_for_period",                     // lock_for_period | admin_release | delay | notify_only | custom
    "lockout_seconds": 900,                        // AC-7b [Assignment] — only when type = lock_for_period
    "delay_algorithm": null,                        // e.g. exponential backoff parameters
    "notify_admin": true,
    "alternate_factors_allowed": ["fido2", "recovery_code"]   // AC-7(4)
  },
  "reset_counter_on_success": true,
  "window_semantics": "sliding"
}
```

The numbers above are an **example organizational choice**; they are not derived from, and must not be cited to, AC-7.

State machine (pseudocode, transactionally safe):

```
function on_logon_attempt(user_id, factor, source):
  tx:
    rec = SELECT ... FROM logon_state WHERE user_id = ? FOR UPDATE
    if rec.locked_until is not null and now < rec.locked_until:
        return DENY_LOCKED(rec.locked_until)          // AC-7b
    if rec.locked_until is not null and now >= rec.locked_until:
        rec.locked_until = null; rec.failures = []     // automatic release after the assigned period

    if verify(factor):
        rec.failures = []                              // consecurity is broken by success
        return ALLOW

    cutoff = now - policy.attempt_window_seconds
    rec.failures = [t for t in rec.failures if t > cutoff] + [now]   // sliding window
    if len(rec.failures) >= policy.max_consecutive_invalid_attempts:
        apply(policy.response) -> rec.locked_until = now + lockout_seconds (or null if admin_release)
        emit audit_event(AC7_LOCKOUT, user_id, count=len(rec.failures))
    return DENY_INVALID(remaining = policy.max - len(rec.failures))
```

Implementation points that are easy to get wrong:

- **Consectiveness is window-scoped, not lifetime.** If the assigned window is T, count only failures with timestamp > now − T; otherwise a slow brute force evades the limit.
- **Reset on success** is implied by “consecurity” and should be an explicit policy flag, not an accident of implementation.
- **Row-level locking** on the counter (`FOR UPDATE` / atomic increment) — otherwise parallel attempts defeat the limit.
- **Emit an audit event** for both the lockout and the automatic release; AC-7 is assessed on evidence.
- **Admin release path** and **alternate-factor path** (AC-7(4)) must both exist if the org selects them, or the control cannot be met as written.
- **Do not log the submitted password** when recording a failure; log the user identifier, source, timestamp, and count only.

## Bottom line for the three asks

AC-7 answers “you must have a limit, a window, and an automatic response — define them.” It does not answer “3 / 15 / 15,” and any document claiming NIST mandates those figures for AC-7 is misattributing organizational or vendor guidance.

swappiness¶
This control is used to define the rough relative IO cost of swapping
and filesystem paging, as a value between 0 and 200. At 100, the VM
assumes equal IO cost and will thus apply memory pressure to the page
cache and swap-backed pages equally; lower values signify more
expensive swap IO, higher values indicates cheaper.
Keep in mind that filesystem IO patterns under memory pressure tend to
be more efficient than swap’s random IO. An optimal value will require
experimentation and will also be workload-dependent.
The default value is 60.
For in-memory swap, like zram or zswap, as well as hybrid setups that
have swap on faster devices than the filesystem, values beyond 100 can
be considered. For example, if the random IO against the swap device
is on average 2x faster than IO from the filesystem, swappiness should
be 133 (x + 2x = 200, 2x = 133.33).
At 0, the kernel will not initiate swap until the amount of free and
file-backed pages is less than the high watermark in a zone.

Swap
zswap
zram, formerly called compcache, is a Linux kernel module for creating a compressed block device in RAM, i.e. a RAM disk with on-the-fly disk compression. The block device created with zram can then be used for swap or as a general-purpose RAM disk. The two most common uses for zram are for the storage of temporary files (/tmp) and as a swap device. Initially, zram had only the latter function, hence the original name "compcache" ("compressed cache").
Usage as swap
Initially the created zram block device does not reserve or use any RAM. Only as files need or want to be swapped out, they will be compressed and moved into the zram block device. The zram block device will then dynamically grow or shrink as required.

/etc/systemd/zram-generator.conf
[zram0]
This is sufficient to get a zram device called zram0 created with the default options (see zram-generator.conf(5) for their current values).
By default the zram device will use half the RAM size but no more than 4 GiB: e.g. it will create a 2 GiB zram device if you have 4 GiB of RAM, but only a 4 GiB zram device if you have 8 GiB of memory or more.
If you wish to change this, use the
zram-size parameter:
/etc/systemd/zram-generator.conf
[zram0]
zram-size = min(ram / 2, 16384)
This will allow the zram device to use half the total amount of memory up to 16 GiB (min(x,y) compares the two values and picks the smallest).
if you want to unconditionally allow the zram device to use half the memory, use zram-size = ram / 2
for a fixed size, use e.g. zram-size = 8192.
See zram-generator.conf(5) § EXAMPLES for graphs and a more complex example.
To use a different compression algorithm than the kernel's current default, use

/etc/systemd/zram-generator.conf
[zram0]

Explanation of the configuration:
These values are what Pop!_OS uses. That Pop!_OS GitHub pull request also links to some testing done by users on r/Fedora, which determined that vm.page-cluster = 0 is ideal. They also found a high swappiness value to be ideal, which matches what is suggested by the kernel docs:
The default value is 60.
For in-memory swap, like zram or zswap, as well as hybrid setups that have swap on faster devices than the filesystem, values beyond 100 can be considered. For example, if the random IO against the swap device is on average 2x faster than IO from the filesystem, swappiness should be 133 (x + 2x = 200, 2x = 133.33).
On a system with a hard drive, random I/O against the in-memory device would be orders of magnitude faster than I/O against the filesystem, so swappiness should be ~200. Even on a system with a fast SSD, a high swappiness value may be ideal.

Example: Assume a system with 4G of swap. A task which allocates 6G of memory
(by mistake) under 2G memory limitation will use all swap.
In this case, setting memsw.limit_in_bytes=3G will prevent bad use of swap.
By using the memsw limit, you can avoid system OOM which can be caused by swap

2.4.1 why ‘memory+swap’ rather than swap¶
The global LRU(kswapd) can swap out arbitrary pages. Swap-out means
to move account from memory to swap...there is no change in usage of
memory+swap. In other words, when we want to limit the usage of swap without
affecting global LRU, memory+swap limit is better than just limiting swap from
an OS point of view.
2.4.2. What happens when a cgroup hits memory.memsw.limit_in_bytes¶
When a cgroup hits memory.memsw.limit_in_bytes, it’s useless to do swap-out
in this cgroup. Then, swap-out will not be done by cgroup routine and file
caches are dropped. But as mentioned above, global LRU can do swapout memory
from it for sanity of the system’s memory management state. You can’t forbid
it by cgroup.

verdict.summary:
Answer for a current mainline Linux kernel on the 0-200 swappiness scale:

1. Accepted range: 0-200 inclusive. `vm.swappiness` is an integer sysctl; the kernel bounds it at 0 and 200, so writes below 0 or above 200 are rejected with EINVAL. On older kernels that predate the 0-200 scale, 133 may be above that kernel's accepted maximum; use the maximum documented for that kernel.

2. Default: 60. This is the upstream kernel default. Verify with `cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness` or `sysctl -n vm.swappiness`. Distributions may override it, but 60 is the upstream default.

3. Value for a swap device whose random IO averages 2x faster than filesystem IO: 133. The kernel documentation gives this exact example:

   "For in-memory swap, like zram or zswap, as well as hybrid setups that have swap on faster devices than the filesystem, values beyond 100 can be considered. For example, if the random IO against the swap device is on average 2x faster than IO from the filesystem, swappiness should be 133 (x + 2x = 200, 2x = 133.33)."

   The model is: at 100 the VM assumes equal IO cost between swap-backed and file-backed pages; lower values mean swap IO is more expensive; higher values mean swap IO is cheaper. Since the swap device is 2x faster, 133 is the documented integer setting, derived from 133.33 rounded down. It is within the accepted 0-200 range and above 100, as the documentation recommends for zram/zswap or faster swap devices.

Apply it:

```
sysctl -w vm.swappiness=133
```

Persist it:

```
# /etc/sysctl.d/99-swappiness.conf
vm.swappiness = 133
```

```
sysctl --system
```

Verify:

```
sysctl -n vm.swappiness   # should print 133
```

Caveats:
- 133 is the correct starting point for the stated 2x cost ratio, not a universal zram setting. If zram's advantage is much larger than 2x, higher values may test better; if CPU compression/decompression cost is material, the effective advantage is smaller and a lower value may be better.
- The kernel documentation notes that filesystem IO under memory pressure tends to be more efficient than swap's random IO, and that the optimal value is workload-dependent. Validate under representative memory pressure.
- `vm.swappiness=0` does not disable swap; it only avoids initiating swap until free plus file-backed pages fall below the zone high watermark.
- If the system mixes zram and disk-backed swap, one global swappiness cannot encode different costs per device; 133 assumes the swap IO actually used is the 2x-faster device.

type: NodePort
If you set the type field to NodePort, the Kubernetes control plane
allocates a port from a range specified by --service-node-port-range flag (default: 30000-32767).
Each node proxies that port (the same port number on every Node) into your Service.
Your Service reports the allocated port in its .spec.ports[*].nodePort field.
Using a NodePort gives you the freedom to set up your own load balancing solution,
to configure environments that are not fully supported by Kubernetes, or even
to expose one or more nodes' IP addresses directly.
For a node port Service, Kubernetes additionally allocates a port (TCP, UDP or
SCTP to match the protocol of the Service). Every node in the cluster configures
itself to listen on that assigned port and to forward traffic to one of the ready
endpoints associated with that Service. You'll be able to contact the type: NodePort
Service, from outside the cluster, by connecting to any node using the appropriate
protocol (for example: TCP), and the appropriate port (as assigned to that Service).

# By default and for convenience, the Kubernetes control plane
# will allocate a port from a range (default: 30000-32767)
nodePort: 30007
Reserve Nodeport ranges to avoid collisions
The policy for assigning ports to NodePort services applies to both the auto-assignment and
the manual assignment scenarios. When a user wants to create a NodePort service that
uses a specific port, the target port may conflict with another port that has already been assigned.
To avoid this problem, the port range for NodePort services is divided into two bands.
Dynamic port assignment uses the upper band by default, and it may use the lower band once the
upper band has been exhausted. Users can then allocate from the lower band with a lower risk of port collision.
When using the default NodePort range 30000-32767, the bands are partitioned as follows:
Static band: 30000-30085
Dynamic band: 30086-32767
See Avoid Collisions Assigning Ports to NodePort Services
for more details on how the static and dynamic bands are calculated.

How Kubernetes allocates node ports to Services?
When a type: NodePort Service is created, its corresponding port(s) are allocated in one

Dynamic : If the Service type is NodePort and you do not set a nodePort

automatically allocate an unused port to it at creation time.

Service, from outside the cluster, by connecting to any node using the appropriate
protocol (for example: TCP), and the appropriate port (as assigned to that Service).

verdict.summary:
Default node-port range

The kube-apiserver flag --service-node-port-range has the upstream default value 30000-32767, inclusive at both ends. Therefore, when the API server is started without any port-range flag, the effective NodePort range is:

  30000-32767

For a Service of type NodePort with spec.ports[*].nodePort unset, the control plane dynamically allocates a free port from this configured range. Under the default range, dynamic allocation uses the upper band first, so the initially allocated port comes from 30086-32767; only after that band is exhausted does the allocator fall back to the lower band.

Static/dynamic split of the default range

Kubernetes computes the band offset as:

  bandOffset = min(max(16, floor(rangeSize / 32)), 128)

For the default range:

  rangeSize = 32767 - 30000 + 1 = 2768
  bandOffset = min(max(16, 2768 / 32), 128)
             = min(max(16, 86), 128)
             = 86

So the bands are:

  Static band:  30000-30085   (86 ports)
  Dynamic band: 30086-32767   (2682 ports)

Check: 86 + 2682 = 2768, which is exactly the inclusive size of 30000-32767.

Allocation semantics

- Static allocation: the user explicitly sets nodePort. The requested port must be within the full configured range 30000-32767 and must be unused cluster-wide; otherwise Service creation fails. The lower/static band 30000-30085 is intended and preferred for such explicit allocations because it has lower collision risk with auto-allocation.
- Dynamic allocation: nodePort is unset. The allocator draws from the upper/dynamic band 30086-32767 by default and falls back to the lower/static band 30000-30085 only after the upper band is exhausted.
- The request-analysis assumption that the static band is the highest-numbered portion and the dynamic band is the lowest is inverted relative to upstream Kubernetes documentation and KEP-3668. Upstream uses static = lower band, dynamic = upper band.
- One KEP ASCII line says 'Static band ends: 30086'; that is an off-by-one typo. The canonical documentation and the worked example table use static 30000-30085 and dynamic 30086-32767, consistent with bandOffset 86.

Direct answers

1. Default allocated range: 30000-32767.
2. Split under that default: static band 30000-30085 (86 ports), dynamic band 30086-32767 (2682 ports).

quotes.whole:
Maximum Segment Size Option
TCP endpoints MUST implement both sending and receiving the MSS Option (MUST-14).
TCP implementations SHOULD send an MSS Option in
every SYN segment when its receive MSS differs from the
default 536 for IPv4 or 1220 for IPv6 (SHLD-5), and MAY send it always (MAY-3).
If an MSS Option is not received at connection setup, TCP implementations
MUST assume a default send MSS of 536 (576 - 40) for IPv4 or 1220 (1280 - 60) for IPv6 (MUST-15).
The maximum size of a segment that a TCP endpoint really sends, the
"effective send MSS", MUST be the smaller (MUST-16) of the send MSS
(that reflects the available reassembly buffer size at the
remote host, the EMTU_R ) and the largest transmission size permitted by the IP layer (EMTU_S ):
Eff.snd.MSS = min(SendMSS+20, MMS_S) - TCPhdrsize - IPoptionsize
where:
SendMSS is the MSS value received from the remote host,
or the default 536 for IPv4 or 1220 for IPv6, if no MSS Option is received.
MMS_S is the maximum size for a transport-layer message
that TCP may send.

verdict.summary:
## Answer

Per RFC 9293, Section 3.7.1 (Maximum Segment Size Option):

| Case | Default send MSS to assume when no MSS option is received | Derivation given by the RFC | Requirement level | RFC 9293 label |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | **536** | 576 - 40 | **MUST** | MUST-15 |
| IPv6 | **1220** | 1280 - 60 | **MUST** | MUST-15 |

**Ask 1 — IPv4 default send MSS: 536 octets.**
**Ask 2 — Requirement level: MUST** (normative label MUST-15; the same MUST applies to the IPv6 value 1220).

### Normative text (RFC 9293, §3.7.1)

> TCP endpoints MUST implement both sending and receiving the MSS Option (MUST-14).
>
> TCP implementations SHOULD send an MSS Option in every SYN segment when its receive MSS differs from the default 536 for IPv4 or 1220 for IPv6 (SHLD-5), and MAY send it always (MAY-3).
>
> If an MSS Option is not received at connection setup, TCP implementations MUST assume a default send MSS of 536 (576 - 40) for IPv4 or 1220 (1280 - 60) for IPv6 (MUST-15).
>
> The maximum size of a segment that a TCP endpoint really sends, the "effective send MSS", MUST be the smaller (MUST-16) of the send MSS (that reflects the available reassembly buffer size at the remote host, the EMTU_R [19]) and the largest transmission size permitted by the IP layer (EMTU_S [19]):
>
> Eff.snd.MSS = min(SendMSS+20, MMS_S) - TCPhdrsize - IPoptionsize
>
> where:
> * SendSMS is the MSS value received from the remote host, or the default 536 for IPv4 or 1220 for IPv6, if no MSS Option is received.
> * MMS_S is the maximum size for a transport-layer message that TCP may send.

(The checklist form of the same requirement reads: "IPv4 Send-MSS default is 536 — MUST-15" and "IPv6 Send-MSS default is 1220 — MUST-15".)

### Derivation of the two numbers

- **IPv4:** the IPv4 minimum datagram/reassembly size a host must support is 576 octets. Subtract the 20-octet IPv4 header and the 20-octet TCP header (40 total): 576 - 40 = **536**.
- **IPv6:** the IPv6 minimum MTU is 1280 octets. Subtract the 40-octet IPv6 header and the 20-octet TCP header (60 total): 1280 - 60 = **1220**. (IPv6 has no header checksum and no variable-length header at the base MTU, but RFC 9293 counts 60 octets of headers, not 40+20+extension headers.)

These are *segment data* sizes (MSS excludes the TCP header), which is why the header lengths are subtracted.

### Requirement-level precision (the part that is easy to get wrong)

Three distinct requirements sit next to each other in §3.7.1 and must not be conflated:

1. **MUST-14** — endpoints MUST implement sending *and* receiving the MSS option at all.
2. **SHLD-5** (SHOULD) — an implementation SHOULD *send* an MSS option in every SYN when its **receive** MSS differs from the default 536 (IPv4) / 1220 (IPv6); **MAY-3** allows sending it always. This is about emitting the option, not about the fallback value.
3. **MUST-15** (MUST) — if no MSS option is received at connection setup, the endpoint **MUST** assume the default **send** MSS of 536 (IPv4) / 1220 (IPv6). This is the ask, and it is unconditional MUST for both address families.

So: the *sending* of the option is SHOULD/MAY; the *fallback assumption* is MUST. The requirement level asked for is **MUST**.

### Implementation recipe (what a conforming stack must do)

```text
# At connection setup, per-connection state:
#   send_mss_default = 536  if address family == AF_INET
#                      1220 if address family == AF_INET6

on SYN_received_or_sent(tcb, seg, af):
    opt = parse_mss_option(seg.options)          # MUST-14: parse it
    if opt is present and valid (kind=2, len=4):
        tcb.SendMSS = opt.value                  # peer's advertised receive MSS
    else:
        tcb.SendMSS = (536 if af == AF_INET else 1220)   # MUST-15

    # MUST-16: clamp against the IP layer's send limit
    tcb.EffSndMSS = min(tcb.SendMSS + 20, tcb.MMS_S) - 20 - tcb.IPOptionsSize

# When emitting our own SYN:
    if our_receive_mss != (536 if af == AF_INET else 1220):
        emit MSS option = our_receive_mss          # SHLD-5
    # else: optional                                 # MAY-3
```

Notes for the implementer:
- `SendMSS` is the *peer's* advertised value (what we may send); the default applies only when the peer's SYN carried no MSS option. Do not use the local receive MSS as a substitute.
- `MUST-16` still applies on top of the default: the effective send MSS is `min(SendMSS+20, MMS_S) - TCPhdrsize - IPoptionsize`. With the IPv4 default and no IP options this evaluates to `min(556, MMS_S) - 20` = 536 whenever `MMS_S >= 556`; PMTUD/PLPMTUD may reduce it further for a specific path. The default is a *ceiling assumption about the peer's reassembly buffer*, not a promise to put 536 data octets on every path.
- The default is symmetric in intent (it protects the peer's receive buffer) but asymmetric in value by address family; a dual-stack listener must select 536 or 1220 per-connection based on the address family actually in use, not on a global configuration value.

### Conformance test vectors

| # | Scenario | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| T1 | IPv4 SYN received, no MSS option | SendMSS = 536 (MUST-15) |
| T2 | IPv6 SYN received, no MSS option | SendMSS = 1220 (MUST-15) |
| T3 | IPv4 SYN received, MSS option = 1460 | SendMSS = 1460 (option overrides default) |
| T4 | IPv6 SYN received, MSS option = 1440 | SendMSS = 1440 |
| T5 | IPv4, no MSS option, MMS_S = 1500, no IP options | Eff.snd.MSS = min(556, 1500) - 20 = 536 |
| T6 | IPv6, no MSS option, MMS_S = 1500, no IP options | Eff.snd.MSS = min(1240, 1500) - 20 = 1220 |
| T7 | IPv4, no MSS option, path MTU drops to 296 | Eff.snd.MSS reduced below 536 by the IP-layer clamp (MUST-16) |
| T8 | Local receive MSS = 536 on IPv4 | Sending the MSS option is optional (SHLD-5 not triggered; MAY-3 applies) |
| T9 | Local receive MSS = 1460 on IPv4 | SHOULD send MSS option = 1460 in SYN (SHLD-5) |

### Scope notes

- The authoritative source used is RFC 9293, which obsoletes RFC 793 and updates/absorbs the relevant RFC 1122 host requirements. The values 536 and 1220 and the MUST level are as stated in RFC 9293 §3.7.1; predecessor documents phrased the IPv4 default the same way but did not have the IPv6 default or the MUST-15 label.
- "Default send MSS" here means strictly the segment-size assumption used when the peer's SYN carried no MSS option. It is distinct from (a) the local *receive* MSS the endpoint advertises, and (b) the *effective* send MSS after the MUST-16 clamp against the IP layer.

directly connected, and for IPv6 this would be 1280.  Using these
fixed values limits TCP connection performance and efficiency.
Instead, implementation of Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) and
Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery (PLPMTUD) is strongly
recommended in order for TCP to improve segmentation decisions.  Both
PMTUD and PLPMTUD help TCP choose segment sizes that avoid both on-
path (for IPv4) and source fragmentation (IPv4 and IPv6).

Low interference potential devices (LIPD) class licence
This class licence lets you use some short-range devices on shared frequencies.
What this class licence lets you do
The low interference potential devices (LIPD) class licence allows the use short-range devices.
These devices include:
wi-fi devices
wireless microphones
garage door openers
telecommand for drones'
radars including automotive
home detention monitoring equipment
personal alarms
ultra-wideband transmitters
infrared equipment
video sender transmitters
radiofrequency identification (RFID)
barcode readers.
All users operate on shared frequencies.
The radio-controlled models class licence is for models (such as model ships or planes) that you control with radio frequencies.
Licence rules
You don't need to apply for a class licence or pay any fees.
But you must follow all the rules in the:
Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025
Radiocommunications Act 1992.

You can find the frequencies for LIPD devices in the class licence.
If you want to use other frequencies, you must apply for an apparatus licence.
Problems with interference or reception
You cannot get protection from interference under a class licence.
We manage possible interference by restricting:
the types of devices
the amount of power a device can have
areas where you can use a device
frequencies for some equipment.
The LIPD class licence has rules about places where you can’t use certain devices. This is to protect important stations from interference.
LIPD class licenced devices must not cause interference to radiocommunication services.

verdict.summary:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — LIPD class licence, 'digital modulation' transmitters, 2400–2483.5 MHz, as in force on 17 November 2026

1. DETERMINATION (answers)

  Ask 1 — Maximum EIRP for a 'digital modulation' radiocommunications transmittter in 2400–2483.5 MHz: 4 W (= 4000 mW = 36 dBm EIRP).
  Ask 3 — Year carried by the name of the instrument in force: 2025 — Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025.
  Ask 2 — NOT DETERMINED. The applicable additional limit on radiated power spectral density is in clause 43, whose text was not available in the source material retrieved. See section 5.

2. INSTRUMENT IDENTITY AND CURENCY (basis for ask 3)

  Instrumment: Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025.
  Federal Register ID: F2025L01047. Registered 05 September 2025. Authorised version F2025L01047 registered 05/09/2025.
  Commencement: 1 October 2025 (ACMA outcomes page: 'we decided to proceed with making the Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025. The instrument will commence on 1 October 2025'; the 2015 instrument 'is due to sunset on 1 October 2025').
  Status as at the relevant date: the Federal Register entry retrieved on 18 November 2026 shows the item as 'In force', with latest version 'F2025L01047 05 September 2025' — i.e. the as-made text is the latest version, and no compalation/amendment had altered the figures by 17 November 2026. ACMA's LIPD page likewise directs users to 'the Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025' as the rules to follow.
  Therefore the year in the citation of the instrument now in force is 2025. (Not 2015 — that is the superseded/sunset instrument; not 2026 — that is merely the date of the question.)

3. TRACE FOR ASK 1 (verbatim from the authorised text)

  Schedule 1 of F2025L01047, table of classes of radiocommunications transmitters (page 29 of the authorised PDF), row 7:

    Class of radiocommunications transmitter: 'Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters'
    Permitted operating frequency band: '2400–2483.5 MHz'
    Maximum EIRP: '4 W'
    Additional limitations: 'See clause 43'

  Operative condition: clause 7(2) of the instrument — 'A person must not operate a radiocommunications transmittter included in a class of radiocommunications transmittters at a radiated power that exceeds, in any direction, the maximum EIRP for the class.' The 4 W is therefore an EIRP ceiling in any direction, not a conducted/transmitter-power figure.

  Unit conversion (for completeness, since the ask is in watts): 4 W = 4000 mW = 36.02 dBm. No conversion is required to state the answer; the instrument itself expresses this limit in watts.

  Excluded near-miss reads — these are the common errors and are NOT the answer:
    • Schedule 1, other table ('Any' generic LIPD transmitters), row 21: '2400–2483.5 MHz / 10 mW / None' — generic LIPD class, not the digital modulation class. 10 mW is wrong for ask 1.
    • Same table, rows 2 and 3: frequency hopping transmitters in 2400–2483.5 MHz at 500 mW and 4 W — frequency-hopping class, not digital modulation. The 4 W concidence is numerical only; the correct basis is row 7.
    • Row 9 (digital modulation, 5725–5850 MHz, 4 W) — wrong band.

4. ADDITIONAL OBSERVATION ON ASK 1

  The 4 W EIRP is subject to whatever clause 43 imposes; the table's 'Additional limitations' column is part of the condition, so a compliant transmitter must satisfy both the 4 W EIRP ceiling and clause 43. A transmitter meeting clause 43 but exceeding 4 W EIRP is non-compliant, and vice versa. This is why ask 2 matters operationally even though ask 1 is answered.

5. ASK 2 — WHY IT IS BLOCKED, AND WHAT THE SOURCE MATERAL ACTUALLY CONTAINS

  The question asks for the 'additional limit on radiated peak power spectral density' for the digital modulation class in 2400–2483.5 MHz. In F2025L01047 that limit is in clause 43 of Schedule 1 (the clause cited in row 7's 'Additional limitations' column).

  The retrieved passages do NOT contain clause 43. What they contain is:
    • 'clause 3  Additional limitation for table item 23 — (1) A radiocommunications transmittter must not be operated if its maximum transmitter power exceeds 10 mW. (2) ... if its maximum radiated power spectral density exceeds 13 dBm per 1 MHz.'
    • 'clause 4  Additional limitations for table item 25 — (1) ... maximum radiated power spectral density exceeds 10 dBm per 250 MHz. (2) ... for elevations above 30 degrees ... exceeds -48 dBm per 1 MHz.'
  These are expressly scoped by their headings to table items 23 and 25 — different classes in the same schedule. Neither may be carried across to item 7. Doing so would be the exact failure mode this determination is meant to avoid: a plausible-looking dBm/MHz number that belongs to a different class.
  Accordingly no value is offered for ask 2; it is recorded as blocked rather than answered on paper. Nothing in section 1–4 depends on it: ask 1 (4 W) is read directly from row 7's 'Maximum EIRP' cell and ask 3 (2025) from the instrument's citation and register entry.

6. CLOSURE PROCEDURE FOR ASK 2 (to be executed against the authorised text)

  Step 1 — Open the authorised text: https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2025L01047/asmade/text (or the PDF at .../asmade/2025-09-05/text/original/pdf). Confirm the header still reads 'Authorised Version F2025L01047 registered 05/09/2025' and that the Register still shows the item 'In force' with no later version.
  Step 2 — In Schedule 1, locate the conditions Part (Part 3) and read clause 43 in full. It is cited by row 7 of the class table and should be headed in the form 'Additional limitations for table item 7' (the same drafting pattern as clauses 3 and 4 quoted above).
  Step 3 — Transcribe the subclause(s) verbatim, noting: (a) the exact quantity named ('maximum radiated power spectral density', and whether the instrument says 'peak'); (b) the numeric limit in dBm; (c) the measurement bandwidth it is expressed per (e.g. per 1 MHz, per 100 kHz, per 250 MHz); (d) any band-edge, elevation-angle or duty-cycle proviso; (e) whether it applies in addition to, or instead of, the 4 W EIRP.
  Step 4 — Report the limit in the instrument's own units first (dBm per stated bandwidth), then convert for any customer-facing statement: mW = 10^(dBm/10). Reference points: 0 dBm = 1 mW; 10 dBm = 10 mW; 13 dBm ≈ 19.95 mW; 20 dBm = 100 mW; 30 dBm = 1 W; 36 dBm ≈ 3.98 W. Do not restate a per-MHz figure as a per-250-MHz figure or vice versa — the denominator is part of the limit.
  Step 5 — Cross-check against the ACMA LIPD page and, if needed, the outcomes paper for the 2025 remake, to confirm no compalation note has varied clause 43.
  Step 6 — Only then is ask 2 answered; the answer must name clause 43 and quote its bandwidth denominator.

7. CAVEATS AND SCOPE

  • This determination addresses only the digital modulation class in 2400–2483.5 MHz. Other classes in the same band (frequency hopping, generic 'Any' LIPD) carry different limits and different clauses.
  • The 4 W is a maximum EIRP 'in any direction'; installation gains (antenna gain, cable loss) count towards it.
  • A class licence gives no protection from interference; compliance with both the EIRP ceiling and clause 43 is a condition of the licence under s.132(3) of the Radiocommunications Act 1992.
  • Currency statement: valid on the basis of the Federal Register and ACMA material retrieved 18 November 2026, showing F2025L01047 (as made 5 September 2025, commenced 1 October 2025) as the version in force on 17 November 2026. If the Register later shows a compalation or replacement instrument effective on or before that date, re-run sections 3 and 6 against it.

blocked_on.why: The additional radiated peak power spectral density limit for the digital modulation class in 2400–2483.5 MHz is set by clause 43 of Schedule 1 to the Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025. The retrieved passages of F2025L01047 contain the schedule table (which only says 'See clause 43') and clauses 3 and 4 (which apply to table items 23 and 25), but do not contain the text of clause 43. The only PSD figures available (13 dBm per 1 MHz; 10 dBm per 250 MHz and -48 dBm per 1 MHz) are expressly scoped to other table items and cannot be attributed to the digital modulation class without fabricating the answer. A value can be stated only after clause 43 is read from the authorised text.

verdict.summary:
# Approved Document B (Fire Safety) Volume 1: Dwellings — sprinkler and common-stair thresholds (England)

## 0. Status of this answer

- **Document answered from:** Approved Document B (Fire safety) Volume 1: Dwellings, 2019 edition incorporating the 2020, 2022, 2025 and 2026 amendments (GOV.UK collection 'Fire safety: Approved Document B', last updated 16 September 2026). The consolidated PDF currently published also collates the 2029 amendments, which are published but not in force; nothing in this answer relies on them.
- **Position stated as at:** 18 November 2026, i.e. after the 2026 amendments took effect on 30 September 2026. The 18 m second-stair recommendation is therefore in force in the version quoted.
- **Jurisdiction:** England only (the amendments state they apply only to buildings and building work in England).
- **Status of ADB:** statutory *guidance* approved under s.6 Building Act 1984 giving practical guidance on Part B of Schedule 1 to the Building Regulations 2010. Following the guidance is not itself a legal duty, but it is the normal means of demonstrating compliance; the legal requirement is the relevant Part B requirement, and a departure from the guidance needs to be justified to the building control body.

## 1. Answers

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Blocks of flats with a top storey more than what height above ground level should be fitted with a sprinkler system throughout? (current published version) | **More than 11 m above ground level** |
| 2 | What was that sprinkler trigger height before the 2020 amendments? | **More than 30 m above ground level** |
| 3 | At what top-storey height should flats be served by more than one common stair? | **18 m or more above ground level** (ADB wording: 'a storey 18m or more in height') |
| 4 | From what date do the changes introducing that recommendation take effect? | **30 September 2026** |

## 2. Basis for each answer

### Ask 1 — sprinklers: top storey more than 11 m above ground level

In the currently published Volume 1, blocks of flats in purpose group 1a with a top storey more than 11 m above ground level should be provided with a sprinkler system throughout the building. The figure originates in the May 2020 amendment. The Department's circular letter of 26 May 2020 states:

> 'The amendments include a reduction in the height threshold for sprinklers in Purpose group 1a (residential (block of flats)) from 30 metres to 11 metres. As a result of the change to the height threshold, Table B4 (Minimum periods of fire resistance) will also be amended when these changes take effect to reflect that a block of flats without a sprinkler system above 11 metres is not permitted if following the guidance in the Approved Document.'

Associated points that matter when applying the 11 m figure:

- **Standard:** the 2020 circular confirms there is no change to Appendix E, which continues to recommend BS 9251 for residential blocks of flats (BS EN 12845 where outside the scope of BS 9251).
- **Fire-sterile common areas:** ADB continues to note that sprinklers in residential blocks of flats need not be provided in common areas where those areas are fire sterile. 'Throughout the building' is therefore subject to that stated carve-out.
- **Consequential effect:** because the guidance treats a block of flats without sprinklers above 11 m as not permitted, Table B4 (minimum periods of fire resistance) was amended at the same time; fire resistance periods should be read on that basis.
- **Effective date of the 11 m figure:** 26 November 2020. Transitional arrangement: the 2020 amendments do not apply where a building notice or initial notice has been given, or full plans deposited, and the building work started before that date or started before 29 January 2021.
- **Subsequent amendments:** the researched 2026 amendment material (whose stated focus is the second stair and evacuation lifts) does not alter the sprinkler threshold; 11 m remains the figure in the currently published consolidated Volume 1.

### Ask 2 — before the 2020 amendments: top storey more than 30 m above ground level

The 2019 edition as first published set the sprinkler trigger at a top storey more than 30 m above ground level. The same 2020 circular sentence quoted above gives the 'from' value explicitly: the threshold was reduced **from 30 metres to 11 metres**. So the pre-2020 answer is 30 m — a figure three times the current one, and the reduction (not a wholly new provision) is what the 2020 amendments made.

### Ask 3 — more than one common stair: a storey 18 m or more in height

The 2026 amendments introduce 'a new recommendation for more than one common stair to be provided in blocks of flats with a storey 18m or more in height' (Circular 'Amendments to Approved Document B (Fire safety)', para 8). The recommendation is delivered by rewriting Section 3 (Means of escape – flats), 'Means of escape in the common parts of flats', paragraph 3.27, which sets out the limited cases in which a single escape route from the flat entrance door remains acceptable — including, at 3.27(a), a flat on a storey served by a single common stair where every flat is separated from the common stair by a protected lobby or common protected corridor (Diagram 3.7), and the further conditions listed in the amended paragraph.

Two drafting points to note, because they change how the threshold is applied:

1. **The trigger is '18 m or more', not 'more than 18 m'.** A building qualifies as soon as a storey reaches 18 m above ground level; there is no extra margin above 18 m.
2. **The measure is a storey height above ground level**, expressed in the same metres-above-ground-level terms as the 11 m sprinkler threshold, so the two thresholds are directly comparable: a block between 11 m and 18 m needs sprinklers but may still be served by a single common stair; a block with a storey at 18 m or more needs both sprinklers and more than one common stair.
3. The 18 m figure is consistent with the 18 m threshold used elsewhere in the England fire-safety framework (for example the higher-risk building definition in the Building Safety Act 2022 regime at 18 m or 7 storeys), which is deliberate — the recommendation is intended to align with existing 18 m triggers rather than create a new one.

The same 2026 amendment package also introduces building design provisions to support evacuation lifts in blocks of flats; those are separate from, and do not alter, the 18 m stair trigger.

### Ask 4 — effective date: 30 September 2026

The amendments introducing the second-stair recommendation were published in March 2024 (updated September 2024) but take effect later. From the Circular:

> 'The changes to the guidance take effect on 30 September 2026.'

and from the Notice of Approval at Annex A:

> 'The approval takes effect on 30 September 2026 except in respect of work for which a building notice or initial notice has been given or full plans deposited before that date and provided work is sufficiently progressed before 30 March 2028.'

Transitional arrangements, stated precisely:

- The 2019 edition incorporating the 2020 and 2022 amendments continues to apply where a building notice or initial notice has been given to, or a building control approval application with full plans made to, the relevant authority **before 30 September 2026** (with the 'sufficiently progressed before 30 March 2028' proviso in the Notice of Approval).
- 'Sufficiently progressed' is defined in the Circular: for construction of a building, when pouring of concrete for permanent placement of trench, pad or raft foundations has started, or permanent placement of piling has started; for work to an existing building, when that work has started; for a material change of use, when work to effect that change of use has started.
- Practical consequence: the 18 m second-stair recommendation is **not** retrospective. Schemes with notices/plans deposited before 30 September 2026 and progressed as above are assessed against the pre-2026 guidance (single stair permitted subject to the then-current provisions); schemes from 30 September 2026 onward are assessed against the amended paragraph 3.27.

## 3. Change log (so the figures are never quoted out of context)

| Version / instrument | In force from | Sprinkler trigger (purpose group 1a) | Second common stair |
|---|---|---|---|
| ADB Vol 1, 2019 edition as first published | 2019 | top storey more than **30 m** above ground level | not required by ADB |
| ADB Vol 1, 2020 amendments (May 2020 circular) | **26 November 2020** | top storey more than **11 m** above ground level (reduced from 30 m; Table B4 consequentially amended) | not required by ADB |
| 2022 and 2025 amendments | 2022 / 2025 | 11 m unchanged in the published text | not required by ADB |
| ADB Vol 1, 2026 amendments (Circular; March 2024, updated September 2024) | **30 September 2026** | 11 m unchanged | more than one common stair recommended where a storey is **18 m or more** in height; paragraph 3.27 rewritten; evacuation-lift design provisions added |

## 4. Application notes and limits of the answer

- **Height measurement.** Both figures are quoted in ADB's own terms — height of the top storey (or 'a storey') above ground level, in metres, measured from ground level. They are not storey counts, and neither figure is a 'more than X storeys' rule. Where the measurement is contestable on a particular site (stepped/sloping ground, storeys partly in roof space, roof-level plant), the ADB definitions section and the building control body's view govern; the figures in this answer are the document's stated thresholds, not a substitute for that site-specific determination.
- **Scope of 'blocks of flats'.** The 11 m sprinkler threshold is expressed for purpose group 1a (residential (block of flats)); the 2020 circular confirms the change was framed for that purpose group, and the guidance covers mixed-use buildings containing flats on the same basis. It does not extend to purpose group 1b (dwellinghouses) or to non-residential purpose groups, which are governed by Volume 2.
- **Guidance, not law.** Both thresholds are ADB recommendations supporting Part B. A designer may depart from them with an alternative that satisfies the requirement, but must then justify it to the building control body; in practice 11 m and 18 m are the benchmarks used.
- **Naming inconsistency in the source material (flagged, not resolved by me).** The March 2024 Circular's Notice of Approval refers to the '2019 edition incorporating 2020, 2022 and 2024 amendments', while the body of the same Circular and the 2026 amendment booklet refer to '2020 and 2022' and '2020, 2022 and 2025' respectively. This is a labelling inconsistency in the published instruments; it does not affect any of the four figures, and the effective date of 30 September 2026 is stated consistently in both the Circular body and the Notice of Approval.
- **2029 amendments.** The consolidated Volume 1 currently on GOV.UK also collates 2029 amendments. Those are not in force and are not relied on here; the answers are the position in force at 18 November 2026.

## 5. Verification trail (sources used)

1. Circular 'Amendments to Approved Document B (Fire safety)' (March 2024, updated September 2024) — second-stair recommendation at 18 m or more; effective 30 September 2026; transitional provisions and 'sufficiently progressed' definition; Notice of Approval at Annex A. https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6605f132f9ab416792eea370/Circular_-_Amendments_to_Approved_Document_B_Fire_safety.pdf
2. 'AD B 2026 amendments' booklet — amendments to Vol 1 and Vol 2 taking effect 30 September 2026; list of amendments to Section 3, paragraph 3.27; stated focus (second stair; evacuation lifts). https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/66d57a94d107658faec7e448/AD_B_2026_amendments.pdf
3. Circular letter of 26 May 2020, 'Amendments to Approved Document B 2019' — sprinkler threshold reduced from 30 m to 11 m; Table B4 consequence; BS 9251/BS EN 12845; fire-sterile common areas; effective 26 November 2020 with transitional arrangements. https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/924446/Approved_Document_B_May_2020_amendment_-_Circular_letter_2020.pdf
4. quotes.whole:
National Tidal Datum
Epoch
The specific 19-year
period adopted by the National Ocean Service as the official time
segment over which tide observations are taken and reduced to obtain
mean values (e.g., mean lower low water, etc.) for tidal datums. It is
necessary for standardization because of periodic and apparent secular
trends in sea level. The present NTDE is 1983
through 2001 and is actively considered for revision every 20-25 years.
Tidal datums in certain regions with anomalous sea level changes
(Alaska, U.S. Gulf Coast) are calculated on a Modified 5-Year Epoch.
*Some locations have diurnal tides--one high tide and one low tide per day. At most locations, there
are semidiurnal tides--the tide cycles through a high and low twice
each day, with one of the two high tides being higher than the other
and one of the two low tides being lower than the other.

National Tidal Datum Epoch
The National Tidal Datum Epoch (NTDE) is a 19-year time period established by the National Ocean Service for collecting observations on water levels and calculating tidal datum values (e.g. mean sea level, mean lower low water). The NTDE needs to be regularly revised to account for long-term effects of land movement, sea level rise, and changes in tidal constituents. Tidal datums and their data are used to generate products and services necessary for safe navigation, coastal hazard mitigation, ecosystem research, coastal engineering, and marine boundary demarcations.
The NTDE Update: New Tidal Datums are Coming!

National Tidal Datum Epoch
 Moving from NTDE 1983-2001 to NTDE 2002-2020
NOAA uses the National Tidal Datum Epoch
(NTDE) to generate the country’s tidal
datums. Tidal datums inform vital Federal,
state, and local coastal zone activities,
including ship navigation, storm hazard
mitigation, coastal engineering, marine
boundary determination, and beach
renourishment.
What is NTDE?
 
The NTDE is a 19-year time period used by NOAA to collect water level observations
and  calculate tidal datums. The period represents one full rotation of the Earth’s
longest [18.6 years] lunar cycle, which influences the world’s tides. NOAA rounds to 19
years to account for seasonal and environmental trends (e.g. sea level change), and
determines the truest average of tidal conditions. By using a common cycle for the
country’s tidal datums, NOAA ensures a nationally consistent tidal datum network from
Maine to Hawaii. The NTDE is managed by NOAA’s Center for Operational
Oceanographic Products & Services (CO-OPS).
Yes. An NTDE update is triggered when the change in Mean Sea Level at the
Nation’s coastal tide gauges averages above 0.10ft (0.03m). Historically, this has
resulted in the NTDE being updated every 20-25 years. However, long-term sea
level trends have shown accelerating rates of sea level rise in many regions (but not
all) of the country. This indicates that the current NTDE update schedule may need
to be accelerated. A more frequent review of the NTDE would ensure that as sea
levels change over time NTDE datums continue to accurately represent conditions
on the coast. For modified datums procedures, which are distinct from NTDE, please
visit tidesandcurrents.noaa/ gov/press/tidaldatum.

Is NTDE Regularly Updated?
A tidal datum is a vertical elevation defined
by a phase of the tide. It is used to set values
like Mean Lower Low Water (MLLW). MLLW
is the average of the lower low water height
of each tidal day observed over NTDE. Tidal
datums reflect an average of all tidal
conditions at a location over time. Every
location has its own values. For example,
MLLW is -0.82ft/-0.251m relative to Mean
Sea Level at Bayou La Batre Bridge, AL but
-3.03ft/-0.925m at North Channel, NY. CO-
OPS maintains tidal datums and bench mark
sheets for 2,000+ locations under NTDE.
As part of the NTDE update, CO-OPS will recompute over 2,000 tidal datums and
bench mark sheets. All new datums and bench mark sheets will be released
online at one time (i.e. NTDE 2002-2020 will not be released incrementally by
region). When NTDE 2002- 2020 is released, new tidal datums and bench mark
sheets will supersede those of NTDE 1983-2001. Data for prior Epochs will
remain accessible on CO-OPS’ website for users.
NTDE data is provided by water level stations that make up the National Water
Level Observation Network (NWLON). While all NWLON stations provide some
data, not all have data that span the 19-year period needed for NTDE. To
account for this, CO-OPS relies on control (tide/water level) stations to infer
what a 19-year average would look like at non-control stations. CO-OPS refers to
this as a 19-year NTDE equivalent datum. This allows all tidal datums to
incorporate data from the same epoch, even if actual observations come from
another time period. 
For NTDE 2002-2020, NOAA will automate parts of its tidal datums processing
for the first time. This involves rewriting sections of datums computation
software and will allow NOAA to accelerate future tidal data computations.
Automation will be needed if the NTDE is updated more regularly. 
 The current NTDE spans 1983-2001. In 2029 it will be replaced by NTDE 2002-2020.

Datum Updates
Tide and water level datums are standard elevations used to reference water level heights and depths. Each type of datum represents a unique phase or behavior of the water along the coast or in the Great Lakes. CO-OPS and its partners are currently in the midst of two large-scale datum updates for the National Tidal Datum Epoch (NTDE) and the International Great Lakes Datum (IGLD).
To obtain datums for a specific location, please visit the CO-OPS Datums Station Selection web pages.
National Tidal Datum Epoch
The NTDE is a specific 19-year reference period over which water level observations are taken to determine Mean Sea Level and other tidal datums (e.g., Mean Lower Low Water). The NTDE has historically been updated every 20-25 years.
International Great Lakes Datum
The IGLD is a common reference system used to measure water level heights throughout the Great Lakes, their connecting waterways, and the St. Lawrence River System. The IGLD is updated every 25-30 years.
CO-OPS water level station 8465705 in New Haven, CT. There are over 200 stations like these across the nation collecting continuous water level data. Their data will be used to calculate the new datums.

Water Level Landing Page
Water Levels
The height of the level of water relative to a Datum.  Most stations with water level sensors provide readings every six minutes.  Some, such as the 1-minute water level stations, provide readings once a minute.  CO-OPS measures water levels at coastal stations and at many stations located around the Great Lakes.  For coastal stations, water levels have a periodic rise and fall resulting from gravitational interactions among the sun, moon, and earth.  For Great Lakes stations, changes in water level are usually due to weather events.

quotes.whole:
Water Level Landing Page
Water Levels
The height of the level of water relative to a Datum.  Most stations with water level sensors provide readings every six minutes.  Some, such as the 1-minute water level stations, provide readings once a minute.  CO-OPS measures water levels at coastal stations and at many stations located around the Great Lakes.  For coastal stations, water levels have a periodic rise and fall resulting from gravitational interactions among the sun, moon, and earth.  For Great Lakes stations, changes in water level are usually due to weather events.
1-minute Water Level Data
CO-OPS provides real-time access to 1-minute water level data to support tsunami detection, warning, and modeling, and support warning and mitigation of other coastal hazards. Data can be viewed numerically or graphically.
NOAA Tide Predictions
A calculation of what the water level will be based on harmonic constituents (see below). This site offers six-minute and hourly tide/water level predictions "on-the-fly" for all stations with harmonic constituents. It also offers high/low data for all stations in NOAA's published tide and current table.

quotes.whole:
Historic Current Data
Each year, CO-OPS measures currents at many coastal locations in order to provide accurate tidal current predictions for the maritime community.  These data sets typically range from one to three months in length and at most locations, data are available throughout the water column.  This page contains the raw current measurements taken during these surveys, which date back to 1997.
NOAA Current Predictions
This new site offers expanded tidal current predictions for stations in NOAA's published tide and current tables.  Customized predictions are calculated "on-the-fly" and are available in graphical and text format.  Six-minute, half-hour and hourly tidal current predictions can be generated for all stations with harmonic constituents. The product also offers predicted time and speed of maximum flood/ebb and timing of slack water (no current) for all stations in NOAA's published current tables.  Predictions can be downloaded in text, CSV, XML and PDF formats.

verdict.summary:
ANSWERS (NOAA CO-OPS, as published on tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov; pages fetched 2026-11-18T00:15:47Z)

1) Current 19-year National Tidal Datum Epoch: NTDE 1983-2001.
   Verbatim, CO-OPS Datum Definitions page: "The present NTDE is 1983 through 2001 and is actively considered for revision every 20-25 years." (https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum_options, sha256 b8c630b36f09)
   Verbatim, CO-OPS NTDE landing page: "NOAA currently utilizes the 1983-2001 National Tidal Datum Epoch. This epoch is now undergoing revision and will be replaced by the fifth iteration of the NTDE." (https://www.tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ntde/index.html, sha256 4fa508e48279)
   Verbatim, CO-OPS NTDE factsheet: "The current NTDE spans 1983-2001." (https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/assets/pdf/NTDE_new_margins.pdf, sha256 efd5780ac58d)
   Length check: 1983 through 2001 inclusive = 19 years, matching the 19-year NTDE definition on the same pages.

2) Water-level data coverage of the replacement (fifth) epoch: 2002-2020.
   Verbatim, NTDE landing page: "Measurements for the update will be based on water level data spanning the years 2002-2020."
   Verbatim, NTDE FAQ: "Data for the NTDE update has already been collected for most stations, except for the 130 19-year control stations. These stations will have collected 19 years of 2002-2020 data at the end of calendar year 2020." (https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ntde/faq.html, sha256 27ea305a13c5)
   Verbatim, factsheet title/body: "Moving from NTDE 1983-2001 to NTDE 2002-2020" ... "When NTDE 2002-2020 is released, new tidal datums and bench mark sheets will supersede those of NTDE 1983-2001."
   Length check: 2002 through 2020 inclusive = 19 years, consistent with the 19-year NTDE definition.

3) Proposed release year for products based on the new epoch: 2029.
   Verbatim, NTDE landing page: "The current proposed release date for new NTDE products is in 2029."
   Verbatim, NTDE FAQ: "CO-OPS is currently scheduled to complete this work in 2029. We will communicate progress on a periodic basis and any changes to the schedule as necessary."
   Verbatim, factsheet margin: "The current NTDE spans 1983-2001. In 2029 it will be replaced by NTDE 2002-2020."
   Sequencing check: 2029 postdates the close of the 2002-2020 data window, so the stated release year is internally consistent with the stated coverage years.

WHAT THESE FIGURES ARE NOT (disambiguation required for correct reuse)
- The "time period of 2000-2040" quoted on the datum definitions page ("The 40 years period will include 2 National Tidal Datum Epoch periods. This time period will be updated every 20 years. The present values are based on the time period of 2000-2040.") is the rolling 40-year window used for the Highest/Lowest Astronomical Tide (HAT/LAT) predictions. It is not an NTDE and must not be reported as the epoch.
- "Modified 5-Year Epoch" datums (Alaska, U.S. Gulf Coast) are an exception applied in regions of anomalous sea-level change; they do not displace the national NTDE.
- The 2029 date is a proposed/scheduled release for the full, at-once republication of ~2,000 tidal datums and bench mark sheets; CO-OPS states the release will not be incremental by region and that it will announce any schedule changes.

CURRENCY AND RE-VERIFICATION
- 'Currently' above is anchored to the harness fetch timestamp 2026-11-18T00:15:47Z, with per-page SHA-256 prefixes given so a reader can confirm the exact text relied on.
- NOAA has revised NTDE schedules in the past and explicitly reserves the right to change this one; before publication, re-check https://www.tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ntde/index.html and .../ntde/faq.html and update asks 1-3 if the epoch, coverage years, or 2029 release year have moved.

ONE-LINE ANSWER
Official U.S. tidal datums are currently based on NTDE 1983-2001; the fifth NTDE will be computed from water-level data covering 2002-2020; NOAA currently proposes 2029 for release of the products (datums and bench mark sheets) based on that new epoch.

Tide and water level datums are standard elevations used to reference water level heights and depths. Each type of datum represents a unique phase or behavior of the water along the coast or in the Great Lakes. CO-OPS and its partners are currently in the midst of two large-scale datum updates for the National Tidal Datum Epoch (NTDE) and the International Great Lakes Datum (IGLD).

quotes.whole:
The kilowatt conversion uses a rounded factor, and it is worth knowing why. The International Table BTU is defined through the International Table calorie of 4.1868 joules, which makes it 1,055.05585262 joules; divided by the 3,600 seconds in an hour, one BTU per hour comes to a watt figure whose decimals never terminate. NIST therefore prints it to seven significant figures, 2.930711 × 10⁻¹ watts, and that is the factor used here. Forty-two thousand BTU per hour therefore becomes 42,000 × 0.2930711 = 12,308.99 watts, or 12.31 kilowatts.
Those two NIST entries cross-check each other, which is a useful thing to be able to verify rather than assume. NIST separately publishes 'ton of refrigeration → 3.516853 × 10³ W'. Multiplying the BTU-per-hour factor by the definitional 12,000 gives 12,000 × 0.2930711 = 3,516.8532 watts, which agrees with NIST's own published ton figure across all seven of its significant digits.
MBH is the simplest of the four: thousands of BTU per hour, so BTU per hour divided by 1,000. The M is the Roman numeral, not the SI mega prefix, which is a genuine trap — MBH is a thousand BTU per hour, not a million. One ton is 12 MBH.

Ton of Refrigeration — Definition & Formula Links


The cooling rate that melts one US short ton of ice in 24 hours — standardized as exactly 12,000 BTU/h = 3,516.853 W, about 3.517 kW.


Updated August 20, 2026




The ton of refrigeration is the ice trade’s legacy unit still stamped on North American air-conditioning equipment: the rate of heat removal that melts one US short ton of ice in 24 hours, standardized as exactly 12,000 BTU (IT)/h and carried in NIST SP 811 Appendix B as 3,516.853 W. It is a rate, not an amount of energy — a “3-ton” unit removes 36,000 BTU of heat every hour it runs, which is about 10.55 kW of cooling.

The unit survives because residential and light-commercial equipment is bought in it: a typical house needs 2–5 tons, and a 10 kW cooling load works out to roughly 2.84 tons — squarely residential scale. Converting between the vocabularies is one division through the watt: BTU/h ÷ 12,000 gives tons, and tons × 3.517 gives kW, alongside the neighboring anchor 1 kW ≈ 3,412 BTU/h.

Tonnage is also where a load calculation lands. A Manual-J-style or EN 12831 analysis sums envelope, solar, internal, and ventilation gains, applies a safety factor, and divides the total cooling load by 3,517 W per ton to name the equipment: a 100 m² office at 24 °C indoor against 33 °C outdoor, with its gains totted up and a 1.1 factor applied, sizes at roughly 1.5 tons. The calculated number, not the floor area, is what picks the plant.

verdict.summary:
CHILLER CAPACITY CONVERSION — 10 TONS OF REFRIGERATION TO kW

STEP 1 — THE OFFICIAL NIST CONVERSION FACTOR

NIST publishes the ton of refrigeration factor in three places, all identical:

  • NIST SP 811 (2008 Ed.), Appendix B.8, alphabetical table:
      "ton of refrigeration (12 000 BtuIT/h)  →  watt (W)  →  3.516 853 E+03"
  • NIST SP 811, Appendix B.9, table "Heat Flow Rate":
      "ton of refrigeration (12 000 BtuIT/h)  →  watt (W)  →  3.516 853 E+03"
  • NIST SP 1038 (2006), Sec. 5.2.13 Power:
      "ton, refrigeration (12 000 Btu/h)  →  kilowatt (kW)  →  3.516 853"

Factor used:

      1 ton of refrigeration = 3.516 853 kW   (= 3 516.853 W)

Basis and caveats:
  • The 12 000 Btu_IT/h is exact by definition of the unit; the 3.516 853 kW figure is NIST's published conversion carrying seven significant figures.
  • Btu_IT (International Table Btu, Fifth International Conference on Properties of Steam, London 1956) is the definition named in the request. Do NOT substitute Btu_th (thermochemical): that path gives 2.928 751E-01 W per Btu_th/h and 3.514 501 kW/ton, which is a different unit and would be wrong here.
  • This is a nameplate (nominal) rating conversion only. No derating, efficiency, fouling factor, or part-load value is applied or implied.

STEP 2 — CONVERSION

      Q = 10 ton × 3.516 853 kW/ton = 35.168 53 kW

Intermediate arithmetic shown in full:
      10 × 3 516.853 W = 35 168.53 W
      35 168.53 W ÷ 1 000 = 35.168 53 kW

STEP 3 — FOUR SIGNIFICANT FIGURES

The input "10 tons" carries two significant figures but is treated as an exact nameplate count in this exercise; the constraint fixes the output precision at four significant figures.

      35.168 53 kW  →  35.17 kW   (4 s.f.)

Rounded to 4 s.f.:

      CHILLER CAPACITY = 35.17 kW

Equivalently: 35.17 kW_th ≈ 12.0 ton; ≈ 120 000 Btu_IT/h; ≈ 120 MBH.

STEP 4 — INDEPENDENT CROSS-CHECKS (both agree to all seven published digits)

  (a) Via the Btu_IT/h factor (SP 811 App. B.9, Heat Flow Rate):
        1 Btu_IT/h = 2.930 711E-01 W
        12 000 × 0.293 071 1 = 3 516.853 2 W = 3.516 853 kW per ton  ✓
        10 ton → 35.168 532 kW → 35.17 kW

  (b) Via the definition in base units (Btu_IT = 1 055.055 852 62 J):
        12 000 × 1 055.055 852 62 J / 3 600 s = 3 516.852 84 W = 3.516 853 kW  ✓
        10 ton → 35.168 528 kW → 35.17 kW

  All three routes give 35.1685 kW, which rounds to 35.17 kW at four significant figures. The stated answer is stable to the last reported digit under either NIST route.

STEP 5 — REPORTING NOTE FOR THE NAME PLATE / SUBMITAL

State it as: "Nameplate capacity 10 tons of refrigeration = 35.17 kW (thermal), per NIST SP 811 App. B, 1 ton = 3.516 853 kW." Keep the subscript "th" or the word "thermal" on the kW so it is not mistaken for electrical input power; electrical draw will be higher by the reciprocal of the unit's COP/EER.

verdict.summary:
COMPLIANCE NOTE — Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 (Machinery) and Directive 2006/42/EC: application date, repeal date, and current status as at 17 November 2026

1. CONTROLLING TEXT
Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 (OJ L 165, 29.6.2023, p.1), as corrected by the Corrigendum published in OJ L 169, 4.7.2023, p.35, and as reflected in the EUR-Lex consolidated version 02023R1230 (current consolidated version on EUR-Lex: 27/07/2026). The corrigendum is not cosmetic: it moves every 2027 date in Articles 51, 52 and 54 by six days, and it is the corrected text that governs. Any reading taken from the uncorrected OJ PDF, or from secondary sources reproducing it, will give 14 January 2027 and will be wrong.

2. OPERATIVE PROVISIONS AS CORRECTED (verbatim, with corrigendum markers)

Article 51(2):
'2. Directive 2006/42/EC is repealed with effect from ►C1 20 January 2027 ◄. References to the repealed Directive 2006/42/EC shall be construed as references to this Regulation and shall be read in accordance with the correlation table in Annex XII.'

Article 52(1):
'1. Member States shall not impede the making available on the market of products which were placed on the market in conformity with Directive 2006/42/EC before ►C1 20 January 2027 ◄. However, Chapter VI of this Regulation shall apply, from ►C1 19 July 2023 ◄, mutatis mutandis to such products instead of Article 11 of that Directive, including products for which a procedure has already been initiated under Article 11 of Directive 2006/42/EC.'

Article 52(2):
'2. EC type-examination certificates and approval decisions issued in accordance with Article 12 of Directive 2006/42/EC shall remain valid until they expire.'

Article 54 (Entry into force and application), as corrected:
'This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union.
It shall apply from ►C1 20 January 2027 ◄.
However, the following Articles shall apply from the following dates:
(a) Articles 26 to 42 from ►C1 20 January 2024 ◄;
(b) Article 50(1) from ►C1 20 October 2026 ◄;
(c) Article 6(7) and Articles 48 and 52 from ►C1 19 July 2023 ◄;
(d) Article 6(2) to (6), (8) and (11) and Articles 47 and 53(3) from ►C1 20 July 2024 ◄.'

3. CORRIGENDUM MAPPING (OJ L 169, 4.7.2023, p.35) — points material to the dates
| Corrigendum point | Provision | Uncorrected OJ text | Corrected text |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | Art. 51(2), 1st subpara. | 14 January 2027 | 20 January 2027 |
| 6 | Art. 52(1), 1st sentence | 14 January 2027 | 20 January 2027 |
| 7 | Art. 52(1), 2nd sentence | 13 July 2023 | 19 July 2023 |
| 10 | Art. 54, 2nd para. | 14 January 2027 | 20 January 2027 |
| 11 | Art. 54, 3rd para., point (a) | 14 January 2024 | 20 January 2024 |
| 12 | Art. 54, 3rd para., point (b) | 14 October 2023 | 20 October 2026 |
| 13 | Art. 54, 3rd para., point (c) | 13 July 2023 | 19 July 2023 |
| 14 | Art. 54, 3rd para., point (d) | 14 July 2024 | 20 July 2024 |
(Non-date points 1-4 and 8-9 correct Art. 6(9), 6(10), 47(2), 50(2) and 53(1)/(3); they do not affect the three answers.)

4. ANSWERS

Ask 1 — From which date does the Regulation apply?
General application date: 20 January 2027 (Article 54, second paragraph, as corrected by Corrigendum point 10).
Supporting chronology:
- Signature: 14 June 2023.
- Publication in OJ: 29 June 2023.
- Entry into force: 19 July 2023 (twentieth day after publication — Article 54, first paragraph; EUR-Lex records 'Date of effect: 19/07/2023; Entry into force').
- General application: 20 January 2027.
- Early/partial application, Article 54, third paragraph (corrected):
  (a) Articles 26-42 (conformity assessment bodies / notified bodies) from 20 January 2024;
  (b) Article 50(1) from 20 October 2026;
  (c) Article 6(7) and Articles 48 and 52 from 19 July 2023;
  (d) Article 6(2)-(6), (8) and (11) and Articles 47 and 53(3) from 20 July 2024.
These partial dates do not change the answer to ask 1: 'the Regulation applies' in the sense of the general, residual application date is 20 January 2027. As at 17 November 2026 the Regulation is in force and partially applicable (Art. 6(7), 48, 52 since 19 July 2023; Arts 26-42 since 20 January 2024; Art. 6(2)-(6),(8),(11), Arts 47 and 53(3) since 20 July 2024; Art. 50(1) since 20 October 2026) but its general regime, including the Annex I/II conformity-assessment and CE-marking obligations for the generality of machinery, is not yet applicable.

Ask 2 — From which date does Directive 2006/42/EC stop applying?
20 January 2027. Article 51(2) as corrected: the Directive 'is repealed with effect from 20 January 2027' (Corrigendum point 5). Because repeal takes effect on that date, the Directive applies up to and including 19 January 2027 and ceases to apply from 20 January 2027. This is corroborated by the Directive's own EUR-Lex lifecycle entry: 'Date of end of validity: 19/01/2027; Repealed by 32023R1230'.

Ask 3 — Is the Directive still in force today (17 November 2026)?
YES. On 17 November 2026 the Directive is still in force and still the operative Union harmonisation act for machinery; it is repealed only with effect from 20 January 2027, i.e. 64 days after the assessment date. Machinery may still be placed on the market under the Directive today.
Two qualifications that do not alter the verdict but must be stated for accuracy:
(a) Article 52(1), second sentence: Chapter VI of the Regulation (market surveillance / Union safeguard procedure) has applied mutatis mutandis since 19 July 2023 to products placed on the market under the Directive, in place of Article 11 of the Directive, including procedures already initiated under Article 11. The Directive's Article 11 is therefore already displaced in practice, while the Directive itself remains in force.
(b) Survival effects after 20 January 2027: Article 52(1) prohibits Member States from impeding the making available on the market of products placed on the market in conformity with the Directive before 20 January 2027; Article 52(2) keeps EC type-examination certificates and approval decisions issued under Article 12 of the Directive valid until they expire. 'Repealed with effect from 20 January 2027' therefore means cessation for new placing on the market from that date, not retroactive invalidation of acts done under the Directive.

5. WHY 20 JANUARY 2027 AND NOT 14 JANUARY 2027 — REASONING AND CROSS-CHECKS
- The three 2027 dates are each the subject of an express substitution in the 4 July 2023 corrigendum (points 5, 6, 10). A corrigendum of this kind removes the incorrect text ab initio; the corrected text is what is published, consolidated and applied.
- The EUR-Lex consolidated version 02023R1230-20230629 prints '►C1 20 January 2027 ◄' in Arts 51(2), 52(1) and 54(2), and '►C1 19 July 2023 ◄' in Art. 52(1) second sentence — the C1 flag being defined on the cover page as 'Corrigendum, OJ L 169, 4.7.2023, p.35'.
- The EUR-Lex bibliographic dates table for CELEX 32023R1230 lists 'Date of effect: 20/01/2027; Application; See Art 54', together with the partial dates 19/07/2023, 20/01/2024, 20/07/2024 and 20/10/2026 — all matching the corrected Article 54.
- The EUR-Lex bibliographic dates table for CELEX 32006L0042 lists 'Date of end of validity: 19/01/2027; Repealed by 32023R1230' — the day before the corrected repeal date, which is exactly how EUR-Lex expresses 'repealed with effect from 20 January 2027'.
- Internal consistency: the Regulation's general application date (20 January 2027) and the Directive's repeal date (20 January 2027) are deliberately identical, so that no gap or overlap arises at Union level; the deliverable's two date values are therefore the same value, not two independent numbers.
- The uncorrected OJ PDF (CELEX 32023R1230 as published 29.6.2023) still shows 14 January 2027 and 13 July 2023. It is superseded on these points and is not the controlling text. Note that a reader who consults the OJ PDF, or a commercial database that has not loaded the corrigendum, will reach the wrong date.

6. RESIDUAL LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER (stated, not blocking)
- Scope is Union law. National transposing measures of Directive 2006/42/EC may have their own repeal/transitional timetables in each Member State; the Directive's Union-level repeal on 20 January 2027 does not by itself fix the fate of national law on any given day.
- No delegated or implementing act, and no judgment of the Court, altering the dates in Articles 51, 52 or 54 as at 17 November 2026 was identified in the sources consulted; the EUR-Lex consolidated version current at 27/07/2026 shows no such change. Should a later amendment appear, it would supersede the dates above.
- EC type-examination certificates issued under Article 12 of the Directive remain valid until expiry after 20 January 2027 (Art. 52(2)); this is a survival of certificates, not of the Directive.
- This is a documentary compliance analysis of the legal text, not legal advice.

7. ONE-LINE ANSWER
Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 applies from 20 January 2027 (Art. 54, as corrected); Directive 2006/42/EC is repealed with effect from 20 January 2027 (Art. 51(2), as corrected) and therefore ceases to apply on that date; as at 17 November 2026 the Directive is still in force.

The IAEA Safety Requirements Safety Standard s Series No. GSR Part 3 (Interim), Radiation
Protection and Safety of Radiation Sources: International Basic Safety Standards, was approved by the

the eye follows the recommendation of the International Commission on Radiological Protection
(ICRP) in its statement on tissue reactions on 21 April 2011.
At the time when the draft General Safety Re quirements (GSR) Part 3 was approved by the
Commission on Safety Standards, the Secretariat was asked to develop guidance as early as possible to
assist Member States in the observance of the new dose limit.
